scenes.narration: A starving orphan dares to ask for a second bowl of gruel — and is thrown out into the London underworld. This is Oliver Twist.

on_screen.question: An orphan who asked for more

scenes.notes: Hook before any title. ~24 words, minimal pauses. Names the book.

scenes.narration: Oliver Twist, by Charles Dickens, published between eighteen thirty-seven and eighteen thirty-nine.

Three things worth knowing before we begin. First: Oliver Twist was only Charles Dickens's second novel, written when he was still in his mid-twenties, and it made him a sensation. It is the book that fixed in the public imagination a whole gallery of unforgettable characters — the kindly, bewildered orphan Oliver, the sinister old Fagin, the cheeky Artful Dodger, the doomed Nancy, the terrifying Bill Sikes — figures so vivid they have never left our culture since. Second: beneath the thrilling melodrama, it is a furious work of social protest. Dickens had known real poverty as a boy, when his father was thrown into debtors' prison and he was sent to labour in a grim factory, and he never forgot it. In Oliver Twist he turned that anger on the England of his day — on the cruelty of the workhouses, on a harsh new Poor Law that treated the destitute as criminals, and on a respectable society that let children starve in the gutter or be swallowed by crime. He wanted his comfortable readers to see the hunger and the filth they preferred to ignore. And third: it is, at its heart, a melodrama of good and evil, and a kind of fairy tale — the story of one innocent, gentle boy, passed from hand to hand through a brutal world, who somehow keeps his goodness intact, and whose mysterious parentage holds the secret that will finally save him. It is dark, it is sentimental, it is savagely funny, and it is unforgettable. A word on that world, because it is easy to miss how raw the book was for its first readers. When Dickens wrote it, a brand-new Poor Law had just been passed that deliberately made the workhouses as miserable as possible, on the theory that the poor would only stop being poor if poverty were made unbearable; families were split up inside them, the food was kept near starvation, and the whole system was designed to punish people for the crime of being destitute. Dickens thought this was monstrous, and Oliver Twist was in part a direct, blazing attack on it, read by hundreds of thousands and genuinely helping to shift public feeling. At the same time he plunged his readers into the real criminal underworld of London — the thieves' kitchens, the slums, the child pickpockets, the gin shops — a world the respectable classes pretended not to see. So let us follow Oliver, from the very moment of his birth, in the cold of a parish workhouse.
scenes.notes: Context: Dickens's 2nd novel; the iconic characters; furious social protest (his own childhood poverty, the workhouse, the 1834 Poor Law); a good-vs-evil melodrama/fairy tale about an innocent boy and his secret parentage.

scenes.narration: Oliver Twist is born in a workhouse in a small English town, and his young mother, a stranger found collapsed in the street, lives just long enough to kiss him and then dies, nameless and unmarried, leaving him utterly alone in the world. From his very first breath he is a parish orphan — the lowest, most unwanted thing in that society, a burden on the public purse. He is farmed out as a baby to a wretched 'baby farm' where the children are half-starved for profit, and then, at the age of nine, returned to the workhouse proper, under the thumb of the pompous, bullying parish beadle, Mr Bumble. Life in the workhouse is deliberate, grinding cruelty dressed up as charity. The boys are worked hard and fed almost nothing — three meagre bowls of thin gruel a day and nothing more — slowly starving under the eyes of a fat, comfortable board of gentlemen who congratulate themselves on their economy. Dickens's fury here is wrapped in savage irony: he describes the well-fed board members, the fat beadle, the comfortable officials, all solemnly congratulating themselves on the firmness and economy of a system that is quietly starving children to death, and all quite certain they are being wonderfully charitable. It is one of the great pieces of sarcasm in the language, and it has teeth, because Dickens means every word of the rage beneath the jokes. The boys suffer so badly that one of them, wild-eyed, warns the others he is afraid he will one day eat the boy who sleeps next to him. So, in their desperation, the half-starved boys draw lots to decide who shall dare to go and ask for a second helping of gruel. The lot falls on Oliver. And so, that evening, after the thin supper is gone and the boys sit whispering and nudging him on, the small, frightened child rises from the table, walks the length of the hall to the master with his empty bowl and spoon in hand, and — somewhat alarmed at his own temerity — speaks the most famous request in all of English literature.
scenes.notes: Oliver born in the workhouse, mother dies; parish orphan; baby farm then back to the workhouse under beadle Bumble; the deliberate starvation; the boys draw lots; Oliver is chosen to ask for more.

scenes.narration: The line that shook a nation's conscience — one starving child, asking for a little more.

on_screen.quote: Please, sir, I want some more.

scenes.narration: The effect is explosive. The master is thunderstruck; the board is scandalised; such ingratitude, such rebellion, from a parish boy! Oliver is instantly branded a dangerous troublemaker, confined alone, and a reward is offered to anyone who will take him off the parish's hands. He is nearly sold to a brutal chimney-sweep who would likely have killed him, before instead being apprenticed to Mr Sowerberry, the parish undertaker. Life there is a little less starved but no kinder: Oliver sleeps among the coffins, and is bullied mercilessly by the older apprentice, a cowardly lout named Noah Claypole, and by the servant Charlotte. For a long time Oliver bears it all in meek silence. But when Noah, looking for a cruel way to wound him, begins to insult and slander Oliver's dead mother, something in the gentle boy finally snaps. He flies at the much larger Noah in a sudden fury and knocks him down. For this unthinkable crime he is beaten, locked in a cellar, and lectured by Mr Bumble — and that night, bruised and weeping and utterly without hope of justice, Oliver makes his decision. Before dawn he slips out of the undertaker's, and sets off on foot to walk the seventy long miles to London, the great city, where, he has heard, a boy might disappear and make his own way. The walk itself is a small epic of misery — seven days on the road, sleeping in fields and under haystacks, begging crusts, footsore and faint, passing through villages where the signs warn beggars they will be jailed. A kindly old lady and a turnpike keeper take pity and feed him along the way, small gleams of human decency in a hard world, a theme Dickens returns to again and again: that true kindness, when Oliver meets it, nearly always comes from the poor and humble, almost never from the respectable and powerful. He arrives at last on the outskirts of London exhausted, filthy, and half-starved, a small country orphan utterly alone in the vast, roaring, and dangerous capital — precisely the kind of lost, desperate child that the real London of the eighteen-thirties swallowed by the thousand into crime and ruin. And it is exactly such a child that the city's predators are watching for.
scenes.notes: Scandal; Oliver branded a troublemaker, nearly sold to a sweep, apprenticed to undertaker Sowerberry; bullied by Noah Claypole; Noah insults his dead mother, Oliver fights back, is beaten/locked up; runs away, walks 70 miles to London.

scenes.narration: A friendly boy offers him food and shelter — and leads him straight into a den of thieves.

On the edge of London, starving and footsore, Oliver is approached by a strange, swaggering boy about his own age — a sharp-faced, grown-up little character in a man's coat, who calls himself Jack Dawkins, though everyone knows him as the Artful Dodger. The Artful Dodger is one of Dickens's immortal comic creations — a child who has never had a childhood, a streetwise little man of perhaps twelve who swaggers and swears and talks like a seasoned criminal twice his age, bow-legged, snub-nosed, and utterly without fear. In another book he might be merely funny; here he is also a quiet tragedy, a bright boy whom the slums have turned into a thief before he was old enough to know any better, and a glimpse of exactly what London intends to make of Oliver too. The Dodger, friendly and knowing, buys the starving Oliver a hearty meal and promises him a free place to stay in London with a 'respectable old gentleman' who will ask no awkward questions. Grateful and naive, Oliver follows him through a maze of filthy, narrow, stinking streets into one of the worst slums in London, and up into a crumbling house — where he meets the old gentleman. His name is Fagin: a shrivelled, red-haired, repulsive old man who presides over a gang of boys, all of whom, Oliver slowly realises, are pickpockets and thieves. Fagin is their master, their trainer, and their fence, sending the children out each day to rob the city and bring the spoils back to him. He is sinister and genuinely frightening, yet he greets Oliver with oily warmth, feeds him, and makes a great game of teaching the boys their trade — a game in which Fagin walks about with valuables in his pockets and the boys practise lifting them without his noticing. Oliver, astonishingly, does not understand what any of it really means; he thinks it is all just a merry game, and that he has at last fallen among friends who are kind to him. This is the dark comedy and the tragedy of the whole middle of the book: the gentlest, most innocent boy imaginable, set down in the very heart of thieves' London, so pure that he cannot even recognise crime when it is laughing in his face. Fagin is a genuinely unsettling creation — wheedling and affectionate one moment, flashing with menace the next, counting his stolen treasures in secret, holding real power of life and death over the ragged children who depend on him for every scrap of food and shelter. He keeps the boys loyal through a mixture of kindness, flattery, and pure terror, and he has made a comfortable living for years out of the labour and the ruin of London's lost children. For a little while Oliver is simply grateful: he is fed, he is warm, he is no longer alone, and the Dodger and the other boys treat him as one of their own. He has no way of knowing that he has walked straight out of one trap and into a far more dangerous one.
scenes.notes: The Artful Dodger (Jack Dawkins) befriends Oliver, feeds him, leads him through the slums to Fagin's den; Fagin the master of a gang of boy pickpockets; the pocket-picking 'game'; Oliver too innocent to understand it's thievery.

scenes.narration: Oliver's innocence shatters on his first outing. Sent into the streets with the Dodger and another boy, Charley Bates, supposedly to learn the work, Oliver watches in dawning horror as the two expertly pick the pocket of a kindly old gentleman browsing at a bookstall. Suddenly understanding at last what Fagin's 'game' truly is, the terrified Oliver freezes — and then runs. But the gentleman, missing his handkerchief and seeing a boy flee, raises the cry of 'Stop, thief!', and it is poor Oliver, the only innocent one, who is chased, seized, and knocked down by the mob, while the real thieves slip quietly away. Dragged half-conscious before a brutal, bullying magistrate named Mr Fang — another of Dickens's savage portraits of petty officials drunk on their own power — Oliver is about to be condemned on no evidence at all, simply for being a poor and friendless boy. He is saved only by two strokes of luck: the robbed gentleman, a good and gentle man named Mr Brownlow, has taken a strange, unaccountable liking to the boy and begins to doubt his guilt; and the bookseller from the stall rushes in at the last moment to swear he saw two other boys do the deed. It is a small, pointed lesson in how the law of the day worked — how close an innocent child came to prison or worse on the word of an impatient magistrate, and how only the chance kindness of one decent man stood between Oliver and ruin. Oliver, who has collapsed with fever, is taken home by the kindly Brownlow, and for the first time in his entire life he is shown real tenderness — nursed back to health in a warm, clean, comfortable house, surrounded by books and kindness. And here Dickens plants his great mystery: Brownlow is struck by Oliver's face, which bears an uncanny resemblance to a portrait of a beautiful young woman that hangs on his wall. Who was she? And why does this nameless workhouse orphan look so exactly like her? For a few golden days, Oliver is happy and safe. For the first time Oliver glimpses what an ordinary, decent life might look like — kindness given freely, with nothing demanded in return. Brownlow's elderly housekeeper, Mrs Bedwin, mothers him; he is given clean clothes and good food and books; and he begins, cautiously, to hope. There is even a plan for Brownlow to hear the boy's whole history and set him properly on his feet. But Fagin has not forgotten him — and Fagin is terrified. A boy who knows the location of the den and the faces of the gang, and who is now in the hands of respectable people and a kindly gentleman, is a mortal danger: one word from Oliver to the authorities could send them all to the gallows or to transportation. Monks, too, has his own darker reasons for wanting Oliver back in the gutter. And so the forces of the underworld, criminal self-preservation and secret malice together, close around the one brief patch of sunlight in Oliver's life, determined to drag him back into the dark before he can be saved.
scenes.notes: First outing: Dodger & Charley pick Mr Brownlow's pocket; Oliver understands, runs, is wrongly caught ('Stop thief!'); magistrate; Brownlow takes pity, nurses the feverish Oliver in his comfortable home — first kindness; the portrait that resembles Oliver (the mystery); Fagin fears betrayal.

scenes.narration: Dragged back to the gang, Oliver is forced into a crime that nearly kills him — and lands him among angels.

Oliver's brief happiness is snatched away. When Brownlow, trusting him, sends him out on a simple errand to return some books and pay a bill, Oliver is spotted on the street by two of Fagin's people — the young woman Nancy, and the brutal housebreaker Bill Sikes. Nancy, a hardened girl of the streets who is nonetheless capable of pity, seizes Oliver in a public scene, loudly pretending to be his frantic sister rescuing a runaway brother, so that passers-by help rather than hinder her — and Oliver is dragged back into the darkness of Fagin's world, while the good Mr Brownlow is left to believe, heartbroken, that the boy he trusted has robbed him and run. Back in the den, Oliver is mocked, stripped of his fine new clothes, and kept prisoner. And now a new and sinister figure begins to move behind the scenes: a strange, glowering man named Monks, who meets secretly with Fagin and takes a dark, inexplicable interest in Oliver — not wanting him robbed or killed outright, but wanting him dragged down, corrupted, turned into a convicted criminal. Why this mysterious gentleman should care so much about ruining one small orphan — paying good money not to have him killed, which would be simple, but to have him debased and criminalised — is a question that hangs over everything, and whose answer lies buried in the secret of Oliver's birth. It is worth pausing on Nancy here, because she is the hinge on which the whole tragedy will turn. When she seizes Oliver on the street and he is torn away from Brownlow, she does it well, convincingly, cruelly — and yet Dickens lets us see the flicker of shame and pity in her even then. She has done the gang's work, delivered the child back into bondage; but something in her recoils at the sight of this gentle boy being broken for sport, and that buried decency, that refusal of her own hardened heart to quite give up on goodness, is already stirring. For now, though, she says nothing, and Oliver is a prisoner once more, cut off from the kind old man who was his one hope, and believed by that same old man to be a common thief and an ingrate.
scenes.notes: Oliver sent on an errand by Brownlow; Nancy & Sikes recapture him (Nancy pretends to be his sister); Brownlow left thinking Oliver a thief; Oliver imprisoned, stripped of his clothes; Monks appears, secretly plotting with Fagin to ruin (not just rob) Oliver — tied to the birth secret.

scenes.narration: Then Fagin and Sikes put Oliver to use. Sikes is planning to burgle a fine country house in Chertsey, outside London, and he needs a small boy to be pushed through a tiny window to open the door from the inside. Terrified and weeping, begging on his knees to be let go, Oliver is forced along through the night at gunpoint, Sikes swearing to blow his brains out at the first sound. In a last whispered moment before he is lifted through the little window, Oliver silently resolves to raise the alarm inside and warn the household rather than help the robbery — a small, brave flicker of the goodness that will not be beaten out of him. But it comes to nothing. The burglary goes wrong almost at once: the servants wake, there is shouting and the flash of a pistol in the dark, and Oliver is hit in the arm and badly wounded. Sikes, cursing, drags the wounded, bleeding boy out, and then, as pursuit closes in, abandons him in a ditch and flees to save himself. Oliver, half-dead, drifts in and out of consciousness through the cold night, and at dawn crawls, barely alive, to the nearest door for help — which happens to be the very house he was forced to help rob. And here the melodrama turns, as it must, toward mercy. The ladies of the house — the kind, motherly Mrs Maylie and her lovely, gentle young niece, Rose — take one look at the wounded, feverish, obviously harmless child on their doorstep and, instead of handing him to the police, take him in, nurse him, and come to love him. There is a tense moment first — the bumbling servants want to hand the wounded child straight to the constables, and only Rose's instinctive compassion, her refusal to believe that such a sweet-faced boy could be a hardened criminal, stays their hands. She pleads for him, and wins. Oliver, feverish and frightened, tells them his whole sorry story, and this time — for almost the first time in his life — he is believed, and for the second time he is lifted out of the darkness into warmth, safety, and affection. It is Rose's mercy, a young woman choosing to trust an unknown, bleeding child against all worldly caution, that saves him; and Dickens makes sure we feel that the whole happy ending turns on that one free choice to be kind. The contrast Dickens draws is deliberate and tender: the same boy who was pushed through a window at gunpoint to commit a crime is, within days, reading and walking and gathering flowers in a sunlit garden, learning for the first time what a childhood is supposed to feel like. The good doctor who attends him, the warm-hearted Mr Losberne, and the gentle Rose become his new protectors, and Oliver's natural sweetness wins every heart in the house. He spends an idyllic spring and summer in the countryside with the Maylies, blossoming out of the starved, hunted creature he was into something like a happy child. But the shadow never quite lifts. One strange, dreamlike afternoon Oliver believes he sees Fagin and Monks staring in at him through a window, there and then gone, as though the underworld has reached out a hand to remind him it has not finished with him. And indeed, unknown to Oliver, Monks and Fagin keep scheming in the dark, Monks growing ever more frantic to see the boy ruined, and the net of the great mystery — who Oliver is, and why his own blood should hate him — slowly, inexorably draws tighter around them all.
scenes.notes: Sikes's Chertsey burglary; Oliver forced through the window at gunpoint, shot in the arm, abandoned in a ditch; crawls to the very house they robbed — Mrs Maylie & niece Rose take him in, nurse and love him; idyllic countryside; Monks & Fagin still scheming.

scenes.narration: One woman of the gang risks everything to save the boy — and pays for it with her life.

The moral heart of the whole novel turns out to be its most unlikely character: Nancy. A young woman raised by Fagin from childhood into a life of theft and worse, she is in every obvious way one of the criminals — coarse, drink-sodden, and hopelessly devoted to the violent brute Bill Sikes, who abuses her. And yet beneath it all Nancy has a conscience and a tenderness that will not die, and the sight of what they are doing to the innocent little Oliver awakens it beyond bearing. One night she overhears Fagin and Monks whispering together, and catches enough to learn the shocking truth: that Monks has paid to have Oliver tracked down and ruined, that he has some deep and secret interest in the boy's destruction, and that he knows the hidden secret of who Oliver really is and where he comes from. She even learns that Monks has got hold of, and destroyed, the one piece of proof of Oliver's identity — a locket and ring taken from the dead mother — to bury the truth forever. Nancy understands, all at once, that this gentle child she helped drag back into the gang is the target of some monstrous conspiracy by his own kind, and that no one who could help him has any idea. Torn between loyalty to the only family she has ever known — to Fagin, and above all to Sikes, whom she loves even as he mistreats her — and her desperate pity for the child, Nancy makes a brave and fatal choice. She drugs Sikes to slip away, seeks out the gentle Rose Maylie in secret, and reveals everything she knows about Monks and his plot against Oliver. But she will not betray the others to be hanged, and she will not leave Sikes, though Rose and Mr Brownlow — now drawn back into the story — beg her to let them save her. When Rose, moved and horrified, pleads with her to leave that terrible life, to let herself be saved, Nancy's answer is one of the most affecting things in the book. She says she cannot; that she is chained to her old life by something she cannot explain, a love for Sikes that survives all his cruelty, and a sense that she is already too far gone, too lost, to be redeemed — that home and decency are no longer for the likes of her. She asks only that her secret meeting be kept hidden, and that if she is ever found out, they will remember she had some good left in her. It is a portrait of a kind Victorian readers were taught to despise and ignore — a 'fallen woman', a criminal's mistress — drawn by Dickens with such compassion that she becomes the noblest soul in the whole novel. She slips back into the darkness, having risked everything to protect a boy who is almost a stranger to her, and asking nothing for herself. And she does not know that she has already been watched, and that her act of mercy has sealed her fate.
scenes.notes: Nancy — raised a criminal, devoted to abusive Sikes, but with a living conscience; overhears Monks & Fagin; torn; drugs Sikes, secretly meets Rose Maylie, reveals the plot against Oliver; won't betray the gang or leave Sikes; refuses rescue.

scenes.narration: But Fagin is suspicious, and he has Nancy followed. The cowardly Noah Claypole — who has himself drifted to London and into the gang — spies on her secret meeting and reports every word back to Fagin. And Fagin, in a cold fury, does the most monstrous thing in the book: he tells Bill Sikes that Nancy has betrayed them all, knowing exactly what the savage Sikes will do, and deliberately steering him to it. Sikes goes home in a black rage. Nancy, waking, swears she never betrayed him, that she only tried to buy them all a better life, and begs him for mercy, holding up Rose's white handkerchief and pleading with him to flee abroad with her and start again. It makes no difference. In one of the most harrowing scenes Dickens ever wrote, Sikes beats Nancy to death in their room as dawn breaks. It is a murder so brutal, and so pitifully drawn, that it became the most notorious scene Dickens ever wrote. In his later years he took to performing it aloud on stage, throwing himself so violently into Sikes and the dying Nancy that he terrified and sickened his audiences, sent people fainting from the hall, and — his doctors believed — strained his own heart so badly that the performances helped kill him. He could not leave it alone; something in that scene, the murder of goodness by brutality, the woman destroyed for her one act of mercy, seized him and would not let go. On the page it is mercifully swift and all the more horrifying for it: Nancy's last act is to pray, holding up the white handkerchief Rose gave her toward heaven as Sikes strikes her down. From that moment Sikes is a doomed and haunted man. Unable to escape the image of Nancy's dead, staring eyes, which seem to follow him everywhere, he flees across the country and back, half-mad, dragging his dog, hunted now by the law and by an enraged public who have heard of the killing. Cornered at last by a howling mob on the rooftops of a riverside slum called Jacob's Island, with no way down and the crowd roaring for his blood below, Sikes tries to lower himself to the ground by a rope looped over a chimney. But at that moment he seems to see Nancy's dead eyes again — he cries out, loses his balance, and falls, and the running noose tightens around his own neck. He hangs there, kicking, strangled by his own rope before the eyes of the whole mob, and his faithful dog, trying to leap to his shoulders, misses and is dashed to death below. It is a grimly perfect end: the murderer executed not by the law but by his own guilt and his own hand, as though the universe itself could not wait for the hangman. With Sikes dead and Nancy avenged, the criminal world that swallowed Oliver begins, piece by piece, to collapse — and attention turns at last to the secret that has driven the whole hidden machinery of the plot: the question of who Oliver Twist really is.
scenes.notes: Noah spies on Nancy for Fagin; Fagin tells Sikes she betrayed them, steering him to murder; Sikes beats Nancy to death (she pleads, holds Rose's handkerchief); Sikes haunted by her eyes, hunted; cornered on a rooftop by the mob, accidentally hangs himself fleeing.

scenes.narration: The secret of Oliver's birth comes out at last — and with it, justice.

With Nancy's revelations as their thread, Mr Brownlow and the Maylies close in on the mystery, and corner the villain Monks, forcing the whole secret into the light. And it is this. Monks — whose real name is Edward Leeford — is Oliver's own half-brother. Their father, long dead, was a wretchedly unhappy man, trapped in a loveless arranged marriage that produced the bitter, vicious Monks, before he later found true love with Oliver's mother, Agnes. The father died leaving a will that would provide for Oliver and Agnes — but only on the condition that the boy grew up good and untainted by crime. Monks, greedy and hateful, learned of Oliver's existence and set out to make sure the boy never claimed his inheritance — which is why he paid Fagin not merely to rob Oliver but to corrupt him, to turn him into a criminal and so legally destroy his claim and his good name forever. To seal the ruin, Monks had hunted down and destroyed the last proof of Oliver's identity: a gold locket and ring that had belonged to the dying Agnes, which had passed, through a thieving workhouse nurse, into the hands of none other than Mr Bumble and his new wife, who sold them to Monks for a bribe — and which Monks then flung into the river. The innocent orphan who asked for more was, all along, a gentleman's son and a rightful heir, deliberately hunted through the underworld and the workhouse by his own half-brother, who wanted him not merely poor but criminal and disgraced, so that the inheritance and the family name would pass untouched to Monks alone. Every cruelty Oliver suffered, it turns out, had a hidden design behind it. And there is one last wonder, the kind of coincidence Dickens delighted in: the lovely Rose Maylie, who took the wounded Oliver in and nursed and loved him with no idea who he was, turns out to be the younger sister of his dead mother Agnes — Oliver's own aunt. The family that opened its door to a bleeding stranger was, without knowing it, his own blood. Modern readers sometimes smile at how neatly it all fits together — the one house Sikes picks to rob happens to belong to Oliver's aunt; the one gentleman whose pocket is picked happens to have known Oliver's father — but the coincidences are the point. This is a moral fairy tale, and in a fairy tale the deep ties of blood and goodness will out, no matter how the wicked try to bury them. Oliver's gentleness, which survived every beating, was never a mystery after all: it was his inheritance, the mark of the loving mother and the good father the world had tried to erase, surfacing in a workhouse boy who had never known either of them.
scenes.notes: Brownlow & the Maylies corner Monks (Edward Leeford) = Oliver's half-brother; the father's will (inheritance only if Oliver stays good); Monks paid Fagin to corrupt Oliver to destroy his claim; Oliver is a gentleman's son & heir; Rose Maylie is his aunt (Agnes's sister).

scenes.narration: And so the wheel comes round to justice, as it must in a Dickens fairy tale. The gang is broken. The Artful Dodger is caught and transported. And Fagin himself is seized, tried, and condemned to hang. Dickens gives him an extraordinary, almost unbearable final chapter, famous in its own right — 'Fagin's Last Night Alive'. The old man sits in the condemned cell of Newgate prison the night before he is to hang, and all his cunning, all his oily power, has collapsed into raw animal terror. He cannot follow the words of the court, cannot sit still, raves and mutters and stares, counting the hours, while outside a vast, jeering crowd is already building the gallows and gathering to enjoy the spectacle of his death. Dickens, who hated public executions, makes us feel the horror of both the wretched man and the mob that feasts on him. Oliver, with Mr Brownlow, is brought to see him one last time — and the ruined creature, half-mad, clutches at the boy, no longer the sinister master but a terrified old man begging to be led out of the cell. Even now Oliver, incapable of hatred, can only pity him and pray for him. Mr Bumble, the pompous beadle who bullied Oliver at the very start, gets his own small comeuppance — brought to ruin and reduced to poverty, uttering his immortal verdict on a legal system that has outwitted him. And Oliver himself gets the ending the whole book has ached toward: Mr Brownlow, the first man ever to be kind to him, formally adopts him as his own son. Oliver receives his share of his father's fortune, is restored to his true family, and grows up loved, secure, and good, in the peaceful countryside, among the people who cherish him. Monks, given one last chance and a share of the money in the hope he might reform, squanders it, sinks back into crime abroad, and dies in prison — the wicked brother destroyed by his own nature, as the good one is saved by his. And the memory of Nancy, the girl who gave her life for a child who was not hers, hangs over the happy ending like a benediction, so that the joy is real but never cheap: this world, Dickens insists, extracts a terrible price, and the innocent are saved only because someone braver and more broken than they are chose, at the last, to be good. The orphan who was starved and beaten and hunted through the lowest depths of London, and who never once lost his gentle heart, comes home at last — to a family, a fortune, and a love he had every reason never to believe in.
scenes.notes: Justice: gang broken; Dodger transported; Fagin condemned, the condemned-cell chapter, Oliver visits & pities him; Bumble ruined (his 'law is a ass' verdict); Brownlow adopts Oliver; inheritance restored; Oliver grows up loved and good.

scenes.narration: Mr Bumble's immortal protest — Dickens's sly dig at the pompous machinery of the law.

on_screen.quote: The law is a ass—a idiot.

scenes.narration: Why has Oliver Twist stayed so alive, nearly two hundred years on? Partly because of its sheer storytelling force — the chases, the mystery, the murder, the larger-than-life villains and the plucky innocent at the centre; it grips like few books before it, and gave us characters so indelible that Fagin and the Artful Dodger and Bill Sikes have become permanent fixtures of the imagination, retold endlessly on stage and screen. But mostly because of the anger and the compassion underneath. Dickens took the people his society wanted to look away from — the workhouse orphan, the street child, the fallen woman, the slum — and he forced them into the light and insisted that his comfortable readers see them as human beings, with souls as real as their own. He showed that cruelty often wears the respectable mask of charity and law — that the people doing the most harm to Oliver are frequently the pillars of the community, the beadle, the board, the magistrate, all perfectly pleased with themselves — while real virtue is found in a thieves' den and a slum. And that goodness can survive, and even shine brightest, in the most unexpected hearts: in a doomed girl like Nancy far more than in the well-fed gentlemen of the parish board; in the Artful Dodger's loyalty; in a servant's rough pity on the road. Dickens refuses the easy comfort of believing that the poor and the criminal are simply bad people; again and again he shows them as human beings bent and broken by circumstance, and insists that we judge the society that made them before we judge them. The novel's faith is finally a tender and hopeful one: that innocence, though it be beaten and starved and dragged through every filth, need not be corrupted; that a child is not born bad, but made so by the world; and that kindness, when it finally comes, can redeem even the hardest life. There are fair criticisms to make — the plot leans hard on coincidence, Oliver himself is almost too passive and pure to be real, and the portrait of Fagin draws on ugly anti-Jewish stereotypes of the age that Dickens, to his credit, later tried to answer. But none of it has dimmed the book's power, because what beats underneath is so true and so fierce: a young writer's refusal to look away from suffering, and his insistence that every starving, nameless child in the gutter is a human soul who matters. It is a thriller, a tearjerker, and a thundering demand for a kinder world all at once — and, remarkably, it helped change the real one, stirring the comfortable conscience of a nation. Read it, and meet the boy who dared to ask for more.
